title: Weekly Top Five Articles: The Unformed Self
author: Bradley, Anthony
summary: Anthony Bradley's weekly digest curates five pieces that, read together, diagnose a culture that has lost the frameworks to interpret what it observes about itself. He moves from the commodification of mindfulness (which strips a spiritual discipline of its moorings and repackages it as a productivity tool), to Fukuyama's argument that liberalism survives only when citizens remember why limits on power matter, to the collapse of serious nonfiction reading as a symptom of declining tolerance for being challenged. The digest's most pointed entry concerns 'looksmaxxing': Bradley uses a PsyPost summary of media-studies research to argue that social-media and self-improvement industries have built a five-stage pipeline that teaches boys to see their bodies as a problem to be diagnosed and fixed, replacing older, community-based rites of passage into manhood with a commercialized, DIY self-policing regime. Bradley's closing synthesis ties the five items together as instances of a single failure: an abundance of analytic capacity with no meta-narrative to give the analysis meaning. The entry on masculinity and body image is the sharpest expression of his broader, recurring argument (echoed in his forthcoming book on fatherhood) that boys are being formed today by commercial and algorithmic systems rather than by intentional human formation.
points: Bradley argues that the wellness industry's repackaging of meditation strips it of its original goal (self-transformation) and substitutes a narrower goal (workday buffering), which is why negative side effects of intensive practice get downplayed.
Citing Fukuyama, the digest argues that liberal societies erode not from external attack but from citizens forgetting, across generations of peace, why constraints on power exist in the first place.

The nonfiction-collapse item frames declining book sales as evidence of a broader shift away from readers' willingness to submit to someone else's argument and vocabulary, rather than a simple taste change.

The featured PsyPost research describes a five-stage 'looksmaxxing' pipeline through which social-media platforms and self-improvement marketers convert ordinary male body insecurity into a diagnosable, monetizable identity category.
Bradley's synthesis claims all five stories share a single root problem: strong analytical tools paired with no unifying meta-narrative to interpret what the analysis reveals.
quotes: Olga Khazan writes that meditation can induce insomnia, anxiety, dissociation, depression, and psychosis.

I chose this article because there's become an entire wellness industry determined to divorce spiritual traditions from their complex historical moorings and sell them back to us as universal products.
Liberty without formation devolves always into license. Anger alone won't fix our politics. We need citizens who know how to order their desires well before they seek to order the nation.
Reading serious nonfiction means submitting to another's knowledge. You have to let someone else's argument, intention, and vocabulary trump your own.
We need to recognize how refashioning masculinity into a regime of body diagnoses and tutorials conditions boys to hate their bodies before they've developed much of a body to hate.

Where they used to learn manhood through rites of passage, corporations now school them in self-diagnosis for a fixable self. First you fail, then you Chavicle yourself out of remediation. The hatred comes first, monetization follows.
The common thread in these five essays is the human ability to observe without interpretation because we can do analysis well but we don't know what to do with what we find.
